title: About
text:
A meandering through data science and engineering adventures in Julia, Python, and R.
My name is Alun ap Rhisiart. By background is in zoology; I have a BSc in zoology and a DPhil (the Oxford name for a PhD) in behavioural ecology and evolution theory. My research was around communication, predator-prey behaviour, and spider web building. As part of that I did a lot of work with computers, including building genetic algorithm models of the rules spiders may use to build orb webs. The predator-prey part was filmed for David Attenborough’s The Trials of Life series, and the genetic algorithm work was presented in Richard Dawkin’s book Climbing Mount Improbable.
Eventually, after some years post-doc research at the universities of Oxford and Basel I left academia to take up a career as a software engineer and trainer. I worked for IBM, Computer Science International, Toyota, and London Processing Centre, and more. I wrote the first XML course for IBM Learning Services and presented it internationally. I then went on to work for 15 years at JP Morgan Chase on the prime record system for the investment bank. During this time, I worked in Smalltalk, Object Pascal, Objective C, Swift, Ruby, and Python amongst others.
Then I made a final transition (and wish I had done it years earlier) into Data Science, Machine Learning and Statistics, and Data Engineering in the education sector. These days I work in Python, R, Julia, and SQL. I spend a lot of time collating data both from internal sources as well as public data sources, and putting it together in Databricks in a Data Vault 2.0 architecture using dbt and Prefect. I build models using scikit-learn, xgboost, and huggingface transformers, as well as statistical models in R, and track experiments using Neptune and MLFlow.
Along the way I have inevitably run into blocks and had to find ways around them. I hope to share some of the solutions here to aid others hitting the same issues, in partial recompense for all the great support I have received over the years.

title: Building LoRA Models
text:
Since 2021 LoRA methods and derivatives (such as QLora, IA3, etc) have become more common. Fine-tuning a BERT or decoder model, even though much better than training from scratch, still takes quite a bit of resources. These techniques leave the original weights and biases alone, and instead attach adaptor matrices to some of the hidden layers. We then just train these adaptors, which are much smaller than the original layers. In my case, it was 0.5% of the size. These methods can be as good on large datasets, and even better (comparatively) on smaller datasets.






Note



With the development of LLMs, such as GPT-4, Claude, and Llama, there is the possibility of using prompt-engineering to get these models to output classifications, even though they were not trained to do so. I used this process myself using Llama Guard to find suitable training data to input into this process (some data had been annotated by an external company, but some categories had insufficient numbers, and the capture process produces a large percentage of false positives). The ability to use LLMs and prompt engineering for zero-shot and few-shot classification is a valuable advance, but I don’t think it replaces training a real classifier. I say this for two reasons:

Tests have shown that using such models for zero-shot is not very accurate. A small number of examples in the prompt increases this remarkably, but if you have many classifications you run into issues with prompt length. See https://www.striveworks.com/blog/unsupervised-text-classification-how-to-use-llms-to-categorize-natural-language-data for how zero-shot performed poorly, but improved dramatically if you can provide 23 examples per category.
Even if the accuracy is acceptable, as I will discuss at the end, LLMs are very large and resource-intensive. It is possible to achieve the same level of accuracy or better with much smaller models that require no GPU for inference and much lower latency.



In this first post, I will go through using LoRA (with some additions) methods to fine-tune a ‘roberta-large’ model on a sequence classification task with 12 labels. A follow-up post will consider how we take this model and make it suitable for deployment in production.
Although there is a lot of documentation on https://huggingface.co it was still a bit confusing at times, since they would switch in their examples from CausalLM models to image classification models, sometimes using the trainer class, sometimes raw PyTorch, and so on. So I will document what I did here. I will also incorporate this into MLFlow running on DataBricks.
We will be training a RoBERTA model using LoRA. See Hu, Edward J., Yelong Shen, Phillip Wallis, Zeyuan Allen-Zhu, Yuanzhi Li, Shean Wang, Lu Wang, and Weizhu Chen (2021). LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models. https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2106.09685
We also follow the OLORA algorithm for initialisng the LoRA weights, as detailed in Büyükakyüz, Kerim (2024). OLoRA: Orthonormal Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models. http://arxiv.org/abs/2406.01775
In addition, we use the rank-stabilised scaling factor algorithm to improve performance while training. See Kalajdzievski, Damjan (2023). A Rank Stabilization Scaling Factor for Fine-Tuning with LoRA. https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.03732

text:
Set up PEFT model config
In this case we want a LoRA adapting a RoBERTa large base model.
batch_size = 10
checkpoint = "roberta-large"
peft_type = PeftType.LORA
num_epochs = 10

labels = ["negative", "Eating disorders", "Suicide", "Mental health", "Self-harm", "Drugs", "Gambling", "Weapons", "Games", "Criminality", "Sexual content", "Bullying"]
label2id, id2label = dict(), dict()
for i, label in enumerate(labels):
    label2id[label] = i
    id2label[i] = label
    
peft_config = LoraConfig(task_type="SEQ_CLS", 
                         inference_mode=False, 
                         r=8, 
                         lora_alpha=16, 
                         lora_dropout=0.1,
                         use_rslora=True,
                         init_lora_weights="olora",
                         bias="none")
lr = 3e-4

Load the base model
Now we load the Roberta model specifying the number of labels for the new head. The huggingface example notebook doesn’t specify num_labels, and it turns out that if you don’t then the new head will have two nodes.
model = AutoModelForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained(checkpoint, 
                                                           label2id=label2id, 
                                                           id2label=id2label, 
                                                           num_labels = num_labels, 
                                                           device_map="auto")


Load the PEFT adaptors
lora_model = get_peft_model(model, peft_config)
lora_model.print_trainable_parameters()
lora_model
This tells me that we have 1,848,332 trainable parameters out of a total of 357,220,376, or 0.5174%. This is the value of PEFT methods: fine-tuning of large models becomes feasible as we are actually updating a very small % of the total.

title: Building LoRA Models
text:
Prepare evaluation metric
In this case we will simply use accuracy, but we could optimize f1, recall, precision, or something else if we preferred.
metric = evaluate.load("accuracy")

def compute_metrics(eval_pred):
    """Computes accuracy on a batch of predictions."""
    predictions = np.argmax(eval_pred.predictions, axis=1)
    return metric.compute(predictions=predictions, references=eval_pred.label_ids)

Set up tokenizer
The tokenizer needs to be the one appropriate to the base model.
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(checkpoint, padding_side="right")
if getattr(tokenizer, "pad_token_id") is None:
    tokenizer.pad_token_id = tokenizer.eos_token_id
    
text_column = "text"
label_column = "label"
def preprocess_function(examples):
    inputs = examples[text_column]
    targets = examples[label_column]
    model_inputs = tokenizer(inputs, max_length=None, truncation=True)
    model_inputs["labels"] = targets
    return model_inputs

The next step is to create the training arguments. Some of the tutorials do this in raw pytorch, but as Huggingface provide a convenient trainer class to handle the loop, why not use it?
from transformers import TrainingArguments, Trainer

output_dir = "dbfs:/FileStore/lora-roberta-large-finetuned-reduced_captures" 
repo_name = output_dir.split('/')[-1]

args = TrainingArguments(
  output_dir = output_dir,
  evaluation_strategy="epoch",
  save_strategy="epoch",
  learning_rate=lr,
  remove_unused_columns=False,  # already removed above
  per_device_train_batch_size=batch_size,
  gradient_accumulation_steps=4,
  per_device_eval_batch_size=batch_size,
  num_train_epochs=num_epochs,
  logging_steps=10,
  load_best_model_at_end=True,
  metric_for_best_model="accuracy",
  push_to_hub_model_id = repo_name,
  push_to_hub=True,
  label_names=["labels"],
)

trainer = Trainer(
  model=lora_model,
  args=args,
  train_dataset=processed_ds["train"],
  eval_dataset=processed_ds["validation"],
  tokenizer=tokenizer,
  compute_metrics=compute_metrics,
  data_collator=data_collator,
)
The output dir is often just given as the first argument without specifying what it is. I found this confusing, so always explicitly label it ‘output_dir=’. On Databricks there are two different ways to refer to filestore locations. It appears here we need the ‘dbfs:/FileStore…’ method, not the ‘/dbfs/FileStore…’ method. The training loop does not create this directory, it should exist beforehand.

title: Building LoRA Models
text:
Next steps
We have an accurate model, but this isn’t really production-ready. Although a RoBERTA-large model is much smaller than even fairly small LLMs (357 million parameters, versus Llama Guard 2 at 8 billion), that is still a lot of 32bit floating point numbers, and is measured in GBs. Latency will not be that fast, it really needs a GPU, and it takes a lot of memory.
To make it production ready I will look at:

Merging the adaptor weights with the base model
Distilling into DistilRoberta (82M params instead of 355M)
Quantizing the weights to 8-bit integers (https://towardsdatascience.com/a-visual-guide-to-quantization-930ebcd9be94)
Converting to ONNX and running ONNX-specific optimizations

This would be described as PTQ (Post-Training Quantization); I will compare with the results from QAT (Quantization-Aware Training), eg using QLoRA. It will still require distillation, though.
That process will be the subject of the next post.

text:
4.7.2 Maximum Likelihood Estimation
To keep in line with the book we will also do this manually, using idiomatic Julia where appropriate.

using Random, Optim, ForwardDiff, ADTypes

# Optim requires arrays of floats, not integers
starts = [550.0, 25.0]

# Objective Function (Negative Log-Likelihood)
function NLL(param, y)
    pop_mean = param[1]
    pop_sd = param[2]

    # Catch negative standard deviations so the optimizer doesn't crash
    if pop_sd <= 0.0
        return Inf
    end

    # Equivalent to -sum(dnorm(y, mean=pop_mean, sd=pop_sd, log=TRUE))
    return -loglikelihood(Normal(pop_mean, pop_sd), y)
end

# Optimize
# We use an anonymous function `p -> NLL(p, y1000)` to pass the data
# autodiff = AutoForwardDiff() calculates the gradients automatically for faster convergence
fm = optimize(p -> NLL(p, y1000), starts, LBFGS(), autodiff = AutoForwardDiff())

# Extract the maximum likelihood estimates
mle_estimates = Optim.minimizer(fm)
println("MLE Estimates (Mean, SD): ", mle_estimates)

# Calculate the Hessian at the minimum (equivalent to R's hessian=TRUE)
H = ForwardDiff.hessian(p -> NLL(p, y1000), mle_estimates)
println("Hessian Matrix:\n", H)

The book now checks convergence, inverts the ‘Hessian’, and gets the standard errors for the parameter estimates. We can do the same in Julia as follows:

using LinearAlgebra

# Check convergence
converged = Optim.converged(fm)
println("Converged: ", converged)

# Invert the Hessian to get the covariance matrix
cov_matrix = inv(H)
println("Covariance Matrix:\n", cov_matrix)

# Standard errors for the parameter estimates
std_errors = sqrt.(diag(cov_matrix))
println("Standard Errors (Mean, SD): ", std_errors)

title: ASM Chapter 4
text:
The Turing.jl model
This is the main point about using Julia for Bayesian statistics. Let’s build the same model in Turing.jl. Here, I’m including pop_var as a variable to track, but not estimate. We do this with the := operator, which defines a deterministic relationship in the model. However, for a situation like this I would normally calculate this after the sampling, as shown below.

A note on priors
As I noted in the post about Chapter 3, while several distributions were introduced I was puzzled that Beta, Gamma, Exponential, and Cauchy were left out, and wondered what the priors would be like in later chapters. What we see in Chapter 4 and several later chapters is that the prior for sigma is Uniform for the JAGS examples, but half-Cauchy in the Stan example. Why is that? The purpose of using a Uniform prior is to be non-informative with a bounded range. However, Gelman (2006) showed that a Uniform prior on sigma is not truly non-informative, it has too much mass at higher values. The Cauchy distribution is the Student’s t distribution with one degree of freedom. The half-Cauchy is bounded by 0 with thick tails, and has desirable regularization properties for scale parameters. However, JAGS struggles with the thick tails, so is often replaced with a Uniform prior in JAGS examples.
Since Turing is a HMC sampler (like Stan), I use the half-Cauchy here and in later chapters. However, the Stan team now recommends using an Exponential prior for scale parameters instead of the half-Cauchy, as it provides similar regularization properties with lighter tails and better computational behavior. Since this is a tutorial and we are following the book closely, I will stick with the half-Cauchy for consistency.

using Turing, FlexiChains, MCMCDiagnosticTools

@model function model_4_4(mass)
    # Priors
    # Note: BUGS dnorm(0, 0.0001) uses precision τ = 0.0001, 
    # which corresponds to variance 10,000 or SD = 100 in Turing.
    pop_mean ~ Normal(0, 100)
    pop_sd ~ truncated(Cauchy(0, 10); lower=0)

    # Add derived quantity for variance if required
    pop_var := pop_sd^2

    # Likelihood (Vectorized)
    mass .~ Normal(pop_mean, pop_sd)
end

# Sampling
model = model_4_4(y1000)
chains = sample(model, NUTS(), MCMCThreads(), 10000, 4; progress = false)

After sampling, we can calculate the population variance from the posterior draws of the standard deviation rather than relying on the deterministic variable pop_var defined in the model.

pop_sd_draws = vec(Array(chains[:pop_sd]))
mean(pop_sd_draws .^ 2)

843.2177099960052


Keep in mind that this is a HMC/NUTS model, so equivalent to the Stan example. To me, at least, the model code is far more readable, and the steps needed to compile and run the model also short, simple, and easy to understand. More so than NIMBLE: no configure/build/compile/compile/run sequence, just define the model and sample. Yes, there is a single function to run NIMBLE, too, but then you can’t run in parallel. In Turing, the sample() function can take MCMCThreads() or MCMCDistributed(). And the model itself has no declaring of types, no defined sections for params and data, and the code is Julia, so it has the full range of Julia functions available. Also, there is no likelihood loop, because it can do broadcasting as normal, so it is even shorter than the JAGS model code.






Note



One thing to note is that, as it is Julia code, the order matters, unlike JAGS. You have to define variables before you can refer to them.

title: ASM Chapter 4
text:
Trace plots
Getting trace and density plots from the chains is very straightforward.

plot(chains; size = (800, 600))




There are lots of other plotting options, shown here: https://juliabayes.org/FlexiChains.jl/stable/plotting
Diagnostics can be any of the following (and more):

mean(chains) # posterior mean for each parameter
median(chains) # posterior median for each parameter
ess(chains) # effective sample size for each parameter
rhat(chains) # potential scale reduction factor for each parameter
mcse(chains) # Monte Carlo standard error for each parameter

and more. We can also add posterior statistics from the PosteriorStats.jl package.
Finally, we can do Prior Predictive Checks and Posterior Predictive Checks. But as the chapter doesn’t mention them we will leave to a later model.

Logical tests
For jagsUI (section 4.4.2) the book shows how to do straightforward logical tests, such as mean(sims[,"pop.mean"] < 597). We can do a similar thing with Turing.

The direct vector extraction way

# Extract flattened vector of all posterior draws (e.g. 10,000 x 4 = 40,000 draws)
pop_mean_draws = vec(Array(chains[:pop_mean]))

# Calculate posterior probability P(pop_mean < 597)
prob = mean(pop_mean_draws .< 597)

0.02525




As a one-liner

# Direct one-liner

title: ASM Chapter 4
text:
Other options besides Turing
The Julia ecosystem is a lot less mature than R. Turing itself is mature and stable, but other packages for Bayesian modeling may not be as fully developed or as user-friendly as their R counterparts.

TuringGLM
I tried JuliaBUGS and TuringGLM as well, and could get neither to work. TuringGLM has just been archived, end of August 2026, in favour of newer packages. It would be the equivalent of brms. It is being replaced by TuringRegressions.jl and/or BayesianRegressionModels.jl, which I have not yet tried. There is also Soss.jl which seems to be a Julia interface to the Python library, so will not be considered here. I will try the other two packages and if successful, I will report my findings here.


JuliaBUGS
If TuringGLM is the equivalent of brms, then JuliaBUGS is the equivalent of rjags or jagsui, providing an interface to the JAGS modelling language from within Julia. It does not call the R programs, but runs on top of Turing.jl. This sounds great for someone coming from R. Even better, it refers to a subpackage in R which would allow R users to run their model in Julia. However, the documentation is messy and I could not get either this simple model to work nor the examples in the documentation. Therefore, I will not be considering JuliaBUGS further in this series.


Gibbs Sampler
It is a shame that there is no direct equivalent to a Gibbs sampler in Julia, as they do make handling of discrete variables such as N-Mixture or occupancy models much easier. There is a Gibbs sampler, but it seems to be for combining different samplers within a single framework. However, there is an argument to be made that marginalisation is the best approach.
I note that Turing does support Particle Gibbs, but I don’t think that is quite the same use case. They provide AbstractMCMC as a common interface for MCMC samplers, which allows for flexibility in choosing different sampling algorithms, and it would seem not too difficult to have a Gibbs sampler for common ecological use cases to be built using it. There is, after all, a Metropolis-Hastings sampler. I’ll look into that possibility.

title: ASM Chapter 5
text:
Chapter 5 of Applied Statistical Modelling for Ecologists, by Marc Kéry and Kenneth Kellner, focuses on Ordinary Linear Regression. This chapter also gets in the interesting subject of Posterior Predictive Checks and Goodness Of Fit.
In this chapter, we use a simulated dataset about wallcreepers (which we don’t have in the UK, grrrh). I guess this is very familiar to most people. If the value of our dependent variable \(y_i\) varies according to independent variable \(x_i\), then \[\mu = \alpha + \beta\cdot x\] We take this deterministic, linear part to be the mean, or expected value. \[y_i\sim{Normal(\alpha + \beta\cdot x_i, \sigma^2)}\] We can also express this as a linear equation for the mean plus an error term. \[y_i = \alpha + \beta\cdot x_i + \epsilon_i\] \[\epsilon_i\sim{Normal(0, \sigma^2)}\] So, we have an overall intercept, a coefficient for the effect of x, which will be a regression line, and some scatter around that line which is normally distributed but centered on the line itself.

title: ASM Chapter 5
text:
5.4 Bayesian Analysis
We will translate the JAGS version of the linear regression model into a Bayesian analysis using Julia’s Turing package. Now we start to see some major differences between the way you would approach this in BUGS/JAGS and how you do it in Turing.
In the JAGS code, you put everything into the model block, including priors, likelihood, posterior predictive checks, derived residuals, etc. In Turing, this slows down or may even break the NUTS sampler. In JAGS, the model string is a scripting language telling JAGS what nodes to track during its Gibbs sampling loops. In Turing, the @model macro defines a strict probabilistic log-density target for the sampler. Everything else, residuals, fit statistics, predictive datasets, etc, is just standard Julia code applied to the resulting DataFrame or Chain (see 5.4.2 below). Since Julia is fast, we don’t have to convert this into a different language such as C++.
NB the @. macro at the start of a statement just means to broadcast each of the operations element-wise over arrays. You can also, (and you see I do) just add the . broadcast operator for each one.






Note



The Turing philosophy is: fit the parameters in the model, generate predictions outside the model.



using Turing, FlexiChains, MCMCDiagnosticTools

@model function linear_regression(x, y)
  # Priors. tau = 0.0001 is sd = 100
    α ~ Normal(0, 100)
    β ~ Normal(0, 100)
    σ ~ truncated(Cauchy(0, 10); lower=0)

  # Likelihood
    μ = @. α + β * x
    y ~ product_distribution(Normal.(μ, σ))
end

n_chains = 4
model = linear_regression(x, y)
chains = sample(model, NUTS(), MCMCThreads(), 10000, n_chains; progress=false)


summarystats(chains)

5.4.2 GOF and Posterior Predictive Checks
To replicate the fit and fit.new discrepancy measures from JAGS, we extract the posterior samples and calculate the sums-of-squares in standard Julia. This approach is lightning-fast and mathematically identical to the JAGS output.


# Extract parameter vectors from the chain
α_post = vec(Array(chains[:α]))
β_post  = vec(Array(chains[:β]))
σ_post = vec(Array(chains[:σ]))

S = length(α_post) # Number of posterior draws
fit = zeros(S)         # Sum of squares for actual data
fit_new = zeros(S)     # Sum of squares for new data

# Generate y.new and compute discrepancies for every posterior draw
for s in 1:S
    # Expected values for this iteration
    μ = @. α_post[s] + β_post[s] * x
    
    # Generate replicate dataset
    y_new = rand.(Normal.(μ, σ_post[s]))
    
    # Calculate squared residuals
    fit[s]     = sum((y .- μ).^2)
    fit_new[s] = sum((y_new .- μ).^2)
end

# Calculate the Bayesian p-value (proportion of times fit_new > fit)
bp_val = mean(fit_new .> fit)
println("Bayesian p-value: ", round(bp_val, digits=3))

Bayesian p-value: 0.53


As with the book, we have a value close to 0.5, so a decent fit.

# Replicate the JAGS goodness-of-fit scatter plot
scatter(fit, fit_new, 
    color = (:black), 
    markershape = :circle, 
    markerstrokewidth = 0,
    xlabel = "Discrepancy actual data (fit)",
    ylabel = "Discrepancy replicate data (fit.new)",
    title = "Bayesian p-value = $(round(bp_val, digits=3))",
    legend = false,
    framestyle = :box,
    aspect_ratio = :equal # Keeps the 1:1 line perfectly diagonal
)

# Add 1:1 reference line
min_val = min(minimum(fit), minimum(fit_new))
max_val = max(maximum(fit), maximum(fit_new))
plot!([min_val, max_val], [min_val, max_val], color=:red, linewidth=2)




Finally, we will plot the Credible Intervals (CRI) like figure 5.4 in the book. First obtain predictions and calculate offset distances for the plot ribbon. Note that in R the plots are built using polygon and absolute values. In Julia we use the ribbon keyword and provide the lower and upper offsets relative to the mean prediction.

using Statistics

# Matrix of predictions: rows = length(xpred), cols = number of MCMC draws
predictions = [α_post[s] + β_post[s] * xp for xp in xpred, s in 1:length(α_post)]

# Calculate Bayesian point estimates (post. means) and 95% CRI
BPE = vec(mean(predictions, dims=2))
LPB = [quantile(row, 0.025) for row in eachrow(predictions)]
UPB = [quantile(row, 0.975) for row in eachrow(predictions)]

# Calculate offset distances required by Plots.jl 'ribbon'
BPE_rib_lower = BPE .- LPB
BPE_rib_upper = UPB .- BPE

    color = :blue,

    linewidth = 2,
    label = "Maximum likelihood"

    color = :red,
    fillalpha = 0.2,       # rgb(1, 0, 0, 0.2)
    linewidth = 2,
    label = "Posterior inference"
)

5.7 Maximum Likelihood Estimation
We will do a more-or-less direct translation of the R code for maximum log-likelihood estimation into Julia.

using Optim

# Define the NLL function
function NLL(params, y, x)
    α = params[1]
    β  = params[2]
    σ = exp(params[3]) # convert from log scale
    n = length(y)

    # Vectorized calculation using Julia's broadcasting dot (.) syntax
    μ = @. α + β * x
    LL = logpdf.(Normal.(μ, σ), y)
    
    return -sum(LL)
end

# Minimize the NLL to find MLEs
inits = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0]

# Wrap NLL in a function for Optim
objective(params) = NLL(params, y, x)

# Run optimization using BFGS
# Autodiff is optional but highly recommended in Julia for exact gradients
out5_7 = optimize(objective, inits, BFGS(), autodiff = AutoForwardDiff())

# Extract parameters
# Optim.minimizer returns the optimal parameters
diy_params = Optim.minimizer(out5_7)

diy_est = [
    diy_params[1],        # alpha
    diy_params[2],        # beta
    diy_params[3]         # log.sigma
]

Efficiency Comparison
In the last section of each chapter I compare the efficiency of the HMC/NUTS model in Julia with the JAGs model in R. All run on a MacBook Pro with M5 Pro chip, 24GB RAM.
I ran the jagsUI model in RStudio and saved the MCMC metrics to a CSV file, which we will read into Julia for comparison. Here is the R code, added at the end of the 5.4.1 section:
```{r}
# Output metrics for comparison with Turing
compare.params = c("alpha", "beta", "sigma")

# Time the whole run (wall clock, includes adaptation + burnin)
elapsed <- system.time({
    fit <- jags(data     = dataList,
            inits        = inits,
            parameters.to.save = compare.params,  # keep this list IDENTICAL to Julia
            model.file   = "model5.4.txt",
            n.chains     = nc,
            n.iter       = ni,
            n.burnin     = nb,
            n.thin       = nt,
            parallel     = TRUE)
})[["elapsed"]]

# Per-parameter effective sample size, dropping derived quantities
neff <- fit$summary[, "n.eff"]
neff <- neff[!names(neff) %in% "deviance"]

jags_metrics <- data.frame(sampler  = "JAGS",
                           min_ess  = min(neff),
                           mean_ess = mean(neff),
                           seconds  = elapsed)
jags_metrics$min_ess_s  <- jags_metrics$min_ess  / elapsed
jags_metrics$mean_ess_s <- jags_metrics$mean_ess / elapsed

write.csv(jags_metrics, "jags_mcmc5_metrics.csv", row.names = FALSE)
```
Back in Julia, we read the R output file and compare it with the Turing model metrics. Here, Turing ran 5000 iterations on 4 chains to make it comparable. JAGS saved 20,000 draws (5,000 per chain for 4 chains, plus 1,000 adaptation). By setting Turing to 5000 iterations it also saved 20,000 draws. This effects overall time, but not ess per second.

title: Stratified train-test-split
text:
A stratified train-test-split function
I previously wrote some Julia code to do a train-test-split with the train dataset also split to train/validation. However, I wanted to improve on this by making a stratified split, which took account of the different sample sizes, giving the same proportions for each label. There are a number of packaged functions these days to this, eg in MLBase.jl, MLDataUtils.jl, MLUtils.jl, and DataSplits.jl. But it was a fun thing to write from scratch.
The data was available in a parquet file with two columns, a ‘text’ column of strings (the corpus), and a ‘label’ column of integers (the labels).
```{julia}
using StatsBase, DataFramesMeta, Random
using Parquet2: writefile, Dataset

ds = Dataset(datadir("exp_pro", "captures_training.parquet"))
captures = DataFrame(ds)
```
Here is the function. As the comment says, splitting the training set into a train+validation set is optional. Note that in my case the labels start at zero (which means false positive). If your labels start at 1 you will need to change the loop.
```{julia}
"""
    stratified_train_test_split(df::DataFrame, split_col::Symbol, train_split::Float64[, valid_split::Float64])

Carry out a stratified train-valid-test split based on the split column name. The basic
split is train/test, according to the ratio `train_split``, which should be between 0 and 1.
 If `valid_split` is supplied, the training set is further split to training and validation 
 (this does not) affect the test split.

 Returns train_df, valid_df (may be empty), test_df.
"""
function stratified_train_test_split(df, split_col, train_split, valid_split)
    shuffled_df = DataFrame(shuffle(eachrow(df)))
    train = similar(df, 0)
    valid = similar(df, 0)
    test = similar(df, 0)

    for i = 0:maximum(shuffled_df[!, split_col])
        df = @rsubset(shuffled_df, $split_col == i) # select rows for each label in turn
        train_size = Int(round(nrow(df) * train_split))
        @info train_size
        mh_train = df[1:train_size, :]
        test_df = df[train_size+1:end, :]

        if isnothing(valid_split)
            train_df = mh_train
        else
            # split the training set into training/validation. Huggingface doesn't do cross-validation
            valid_size = Int(round(nrow(mh_train) * valid_split))
            valid_df = mh_train[valid_size+1:end, :]
            train_df = mh_train[1:valid_size, :]
        end

        train = vcat(train, train_df)
        test = vcat(test, test_df)
        valid = vcat(valid, valid_df)
    end
    train = DataFrame(shuffle(eachrow(train)))
    valid = DataFrame(shuffle(eachrow(valid)))
    test = DataFrame(shuffle(eachrow(test)))
    return train, valid, test
end
```
Now we can use the function to split the data into 80% training and 20% test rows (independently for each label), and further to split off 15% of the training rows into a validation set. Finally, I write each out to a Parquet file.
```{julia}
train, valid, test = stratified_train_test_split(captures, :label, 0.8, 0.85)

writefile(datadir("exp_pro", "train.parquet"), train)
writefile(datadir("exp_pro", "test.parquet"), test)
writefile(datadir("exp_pro", "valid.parquet"), valid)
```

title: ASM Chapter 3
text:
Applied Statistical Modelling for Ecologists (ASM) by Marc Kéry & Kenneth F. Kellner is a fantastic resource for quantitative ecologists looking to deepen their understanding of statistical modeling techniques. It is not as ‘advanced’ as Applied Hierarchical Modeling for Ecology vols 1 & 2 (AHM), or Integrated Population Models (IPM), but it provides a solid foundation for understanding and applying statistical models in ecological research. It takes a Rosetta Stone approach, with examples in JAGS, Stan, NIMBLE, TMB, and ‘DIY-MLE’. But, what statistical Rosetta Stone is complete without a Julia implementation? You could argue the same about a Python implementation, but although I commonly use Python for data engineering and Machine Learning tasks, I never use it for statistics, so I will leave that to someone else.
When I read for my BSc there was a course in statistics, and I enjoyed it because it was very practical. It was statistics that let me make sense of the data I collected and draw conclusions. Back then, it was all about using a cookbook, namely Biometry by Sokal & Rohlf. Inside the front and rear covers was a table, which you would consult to see, depending on number of variables and type of variables, which type of Null Hypothesis Significance Test (NHST) you should use: t-test, X-square, ANOVA, ANCOVA, etc. Each had its own table for looking up the significance level.
It was only when I started diving into Bayesian methods around 6 years ago that I realised these were pretty much all just variations of the same thing: linear models. What the ASM book emphasises is not only are the different frequentist methods related in this way (via GLM), but that Frequentist (Maximum Likelihood Estimation) and Bayesian methods are also related, via the likelihood function. This is the subject of Chapter 2, which I’ll write about later.
It is not my intention to repeat the explanations in ASM, but just to add Julia to the Rosetta stone approach, with some remarks where I was struck by something. Therefore, if you don’t have the book this section may be of little use to you. For those with the book, I give section numbers so that you can match up the Julia code with the corresponding sections in the book.
Of course, Julia has RCall, and anything done in the book can be done in a Julia program, combining the speed of Julia for data munging with the exact statistical capabilities of R. I enjoy working in R, but I also appreciate the performance and flexibility that Julia offers.




This chapter starts a discussion of the common distributions, namely Gaussian, Binomial/Bernoulli, Poisson, and Uniform. Interestingly, not Exponential, Laplace, Beta, Gamma, or half-Cauchy. That makes me interested to see the Bayesian models later in the book, to see what priors they are using.
To start we import the Julia packages, for functions that are built-in to R.

using Pkg

Pkg.add("GLM")

The chapter starts with the Gaussian, or Normal, distribution. This is determined by two parameters, the mean and the standard deviation. In Julia we can directly use Greek letters, not a romanised word.

n = 100_000
μ = 600
σ = 30

sample = rand(Normal(μ, σ), n)
histogram(sample, bins=60, normalize=:pdf)




The rest follow a similar pattern, but note that the way you get a random sample is different from R. There are no ‘r’, ’d’, ‘p’, or ’q’ functions as in R; instead, you use the rand function for sampling.



The Uniform distribution is defined by two parameters which are the minimum and maximum values over which we want equal probability.

A Bernoulli distribution occurs when a binary event can occur with probabilty p, such as a coin toss. If there is a succesion of Bernoulli trials, each with the same probability of success, this is a Binomial distribution. In the book they graph proportions rather than frequencies, and I do the same here. Note the difference from Poisson. Although both deal with an integer, perhaps a count, in the Binomial case there is a strict upper limit. For example in capture-recapture you can’t recapture more than you captured in the first place (the upper limit is the number of trials).

n = 100_000
N = 16
p = 0.8

# Draw random numbers
samp = rand(Binomial(N, p), n)

# Calculate relative frequencies (Equivalent to table(sample)/n)
pm = proportionmap(samp)

# Extract and sort the keys and values for plotting
x_vals = sort(collect(keys(pm)))
y_vals = [pm[k] for k in x_vals]

# Plot them
bar(x_vals, y_vals,
    bar_width=0.4,          # Equivalent to lwd = 20 (adjust to taste)
    color=(:black),    
    linecolor=:transparent, # Removes borders to match R's flat lines
    xlims=(0, 16),
    ylabel="Probability",
    framestyle=:axes,       
    legend=false,
    xlabel="sample"
)

In the book they use R’s model.matrix() function to show the design matrix, which is very valuable for really understanding what is going on, and how categorical variables and continous variables can coexist in the same model framework. There isn’t a direct counterpart to that in Julia, so we make one. R’s matrices can have column labels, whereas Julia’s standard matrices do not, so we wrap the matrix in a DataFrame to retain the column names. The default DataFrame column names are of the form ‘reg:1’, ‘pop:2’, etc so we replace the ‘:’ with an empty string to make them match the R function output.

function design_matrix_df(formula, df)
    mf = ModelFrame(formula, df)
    mm = modelmatrix(mf) # shorthand for ModelMatrix(mf).m
    col_names = replace.(string.(coefnames(mf.f.rhs)), ": " => "")
    return DataFrame(mm, col_names)
end

The outputs are equivalent. In the effect parameterization, the intercept represents the mean of the reference group, whereas in the means parameterization, each coefficient represents the mean of the corresponding group. So in effect parameterisation the average mass of snakes in the ‘default’ region 1 is 65, and region 2 we see ‘35’. That 35 is the difference from region one, not the mass itself. In means parameterization, the average mass of snakes in region 1 is still 65, but in region 2 it is 100, which is 65 + 35.
Effect parameterization is best when you are interested in the differences between groups, and means parameterization is best when you are interested in the actual group means.

Next, we look at a centered version. In R there is an I() operator. Generally, in formula syntax, +, -, and * characters have special meanings, so you need to wrap arithmetic expressions in I() to indicate they should be interpreted “as is”. In Julia, this does not exist. You can use any Julia function in the formula directly, but vectorised operations are not the same, so it is better to add a column with the centered values to the DataFrame. Rather than change the dataframe we use @chain to do it dynamically.

m_centered = @chain df begin
    @transform(:length_c = :length .- mean(:length))
    lm(@formula(mass ~ length_c), _)
end

    markershape=:circle,       # pch = 16 (solid circle)

    markerstrokewidth=0,       # Removes outline to match pch = 16
    ylims=(40, 120),
    framestyle=:axes,          # frame = FALSE (removes top and right box edges)
    legend=false,               # R base plot doesn't draw a legend automatically
    ylabel="Mass",
    xlabel="Length"
)

# Add Regression Lines (equivalent to R's `abline(...)`)
# The idiomatic Julia way to do `abline` is to plot an anonymous function: x -> intercept + slope * x

text:
This chapter starts a discussion of the common distributions, namely Gaussian, Binomial/Bernoulli, Poisson, and Uniform. Interestingly, not Exponential, Laplace, Beta, Gamma, or half-Cauchy. That makes me interested to see the Bayesian models later in the book, to see what priors they are using.
To start we import the Julia packages, for functions that are built-in to R.

using Pkg

Pkg.add("GLM")
Pkg.add("DataFramesMeta")

using GLM, DataFramesMeta, StatsBase, StatsPlots, CategoricalArrays, Distributions

The chapter starts with the Gaussian, or Normal, distribution. This is determined by two parameters, the mean and the standard deviation. In Julia we can directly use Greek letters, not a romanised word.

n = 100_000
μ = 600
σ = 30

sample = rand(Normal(μ, σ), n)
histogram(sample, bins=60, normalize=:pdf)




The rest follow a similar pattern, but note that the way you get a random sample is different from R. There are no ‘r’, ’d’, ‘p’, or ’q’ functions as in R; instead, you use the rand function for sampling.



The Uniform distribution is defined by two parameters which are the minimum and maximum values over which we want equal probability.

n = 100_000
a = lower_limit = 0
b = upper_limit = 10

sample = rand(Uniform(a, b), n)
histogram(sample, color = "grey", breaks=30)







A Bernoulli distribution occurs when a binary event can occur with probabilty p, such as a coin toss. If there is a succesion of Bernoulli trials, each with the same probability of success, this is a Binomial distribution. In the book they graph proportions rather than frequencies, and I do the same here. Note the difference from Poisson. Although both deal with an integer, perhaps a count, in the Binomial case there is a strict upper limit. For example in capture-recapture you can’t recapture more than you captured in the first place (the upper limit is the number of trials).

n = 100_000
N = 16
p = 0.8

# Draw random numbers
samp = rand(Binomial(N, p), n)

# Calculate relative frequencies (Equivalent to table(sample)/n)
pm = proportionmap(samp)

# Extract and sort the keys and values for plotting
x_vals = sort(collect(keys(pm)))
y_vals = [pm[k] for k in x_vals]

# Plot them
bar(x_vals, y_vals,
    bar_width=0.4,          # Equivalent to lwd = 20 (adjust to taste)
    color=(:black),    
    linecolor=:transparent, # Removes borders to match R's flat lines
    xlims=(0, 16),
    ylabel="Probability",
    framestyle=:axes,       
    legend=false,
    xlabel="sample"
)




Here is a simpler approach; we don’t have to expose the proportions calculations as histogram() can normalise by itself

histogram(samp,
    normalize=:probability,
    bins=-0.5:1:16.5,       # Forces bins to center exactly on integers
    bar_width=0.4,
    color=(:black),
    linecolor=:transparent,
    xlims=(0, 16),
    ylabel="Probability",
    xlabel="sample",
    framestyle=:axes,
    legend=false
)







The Poisson distribution is very useful in ecology, where we are often dealing with counts with no upper limit and where the events occur independently.

λ = 5
samp = rand(Poisson(λ), n)

histogram(samp,
    normalize=:probability,
    bins=-0.5:1:15.5,       # Forces bins to center exactly on integers
    bar_width=0.4,
    color=(:black),
    linecolor=:transparent,
    xlims=(0, 15),
    ylabel="Probability",
    xlabel="sample",
    framestyle=:axes,
    legend=false
)








This section shows beautifully how tests that I used to think were separate are actually all related. I must admit that I have never been exposed to design matrices before, and they make it crystal clear exactly what is happening.

In the book they use R’s model.matrix() function to show the design matrix, which is very valuable for really understanding what is going on, and how categorical variables and continous variables can coexist in the same model framework. There isn’t a direct counterpart to that in Julia, so we make one. R’s matrices can have column labels, whereas Julia’s standard matrices do not, so we wrap the matrix in a DataFrame to retain the column names. The default DataFrame column names are of the form ‘reg:1’, ‘pop:2’, etc so we replace the ‘:’ with an empty string to make them match the R function output.

function design_matrix_df(formula, df)
    mf = ModelFrame(formula, df)
    mm = modelmatrix(mf) # shorthand for ModelMatrix(mf).m
    col_names = replace.(string.(coefnames(mf.f.rhs)), ": " => "")
    return DataFrame(mm, col_names)
end

title: Dealing with multi-class ML data
text: For the purpose of child safeguarding, one thing I do is build NLP models that classify texts according to certain risk categories (eating disorders, suicide ideation, drugs, gambling, etc). For this purpose I needed to take text data that was captured (either written or viewed) and have an external annotation company label the texts for me. This was meant to be via Amazon Ground Truth, but because of some issues with the setup at the time I ended up dealing directly with the annotation company.

title: Dealing with multi-class ML data
text: For the purpose of child safeguarding, one thing I do is build NLP models that classify texts according to certain risk categories (eating disorders, suicide ideation, drugs, gambling, etc). For this purpose I needed to take text data that was captured (either written or viewed) and have an external annotation company label the texts for me. This was meant to be via Amazon Ground Truth, but because of some issues with the setup at the time I ended up dealing directly with the annotation company.

title: Dealing with multi-class ML data
text:
The data
The data came back in two spreadsheets. Each sentence had been checked by three separate annotators, and the ones where everybody agreed on the classifications went into a ‘consensus’ spreadsheet; where there was disagreement it appears a fourth person (a supervisor) checked and decided which classifications should stand, and this data came in a ‘noconsensus’ spreadsheet. Note the plural: I asked them to assign all applicable classifications to a text, not just the primary one. A sentence could be about both ‘mental health’ and ‘drug use’, for example. I did a spot check of a good number of the 40,000 sentences, and was very pleased with the accuracy of the result (which is to say, I agreed with their decisions). Nonetheless, there were some data engineering challenges to get the data into a suitable format (there always are!).

title: Dealing with multi-class ML data
text:
Eyeballing the data
The data was of of the form











id
data_x
label1
label2
label3
Final Label




1
“Sample text”
[‘negative’]
[‘drugs’]
[‘drugs’, ‘mental health’]
[‘drugs’]


2
“another sample”
[‘drugs’]
[‘suicide’]
[‘drugs’]
[‘drugs’]



The label columns were in the form of a string such as: “[‘suicide’, ‘mental health’, ‘self-harm’]”
This may look like an array of strings, but it was actually just a single string starting and ending with a square bracket. This would need to be parsed and the strings converted to integer labels.
The first thing I found is that there are some inconsistencies in the labels field. For example:

typos such as ‘suicide’ vs ‘sucide’
differences in case (‘Weapon’ vs ‘weapon’)
some were plural, some were singular (‘weapon’ vs ‘weapons’)
and we had both ‘self-harm’ and ‘self harm’ and ‘Games’ vs ‘Games.’ (a tricky one this because of the next issue)
sometimes the separator was a period instead of a comma
The column names were not valid Julia dataframe column identifiers, for example ‘Final Label’.
In some cases there was an extra bracket in the list of labels, “[‘label1’, ‘label2’, ‘label3’]]” (this one was rare, so it was cleaned up in Excel and re-exported to csv).
Some of the labels had missing quotes, [‘label1’, ‘label2, label3’]

title: Dealing with multi-class ML data
text:
Loading and separating the data
First load it, dealing with the column names in the process. I use DrWatson to set up my Julia projects.
```{julia}
using DrWatson
quickactivate(@__DIR__)
using CSV, StatsBase, DataFramesMeta, Parquet, Random, JSONTables

consensus = CSV.read(datadir("import", "consensus.csv"), header=1, ignoreemptyrows=true, normalizenames=true, DataFrame)
nonconsensus = CSV.read(datadir("import", "noconsensus.csv"), header=1, ignoreemptyrows=true, normalizenames=true, DataFrame)

df = vcat(consensus, nonconsensus)
```

title: Dealing with multi-class ML data
text:
Single label classifier
Now we have it all in one datafame, the next step is to extract the texts that are associated with a classification. This is actually quite simple in Julia:
```{julia}
negatives = filter(rows -> occursin.("negative", lowercase(rows.Final_Label)), df)
self_harm = filter(rows -> occursin.("self", lowercase(rows.Final_Label)), df)
```
and so on for all the categories. Here we don’t have to worry about issues like singular or plural, or what separators are used. The final list is going to be a bit more than the original count, since there are some texts that belong to more than one classification. In this case, only 7% of the texts were associated with more than one classification, and we are not sure whether a multi-class model is needed at all.
```{julia}
total = nrow(negatives) + nrow(self_harm) # +...etc
```

Adding back the labels
We have the texts separated, now we want to add an integer label rather than the text label. While we are at it, drop any unnecessary columns and rename ‘data_x’ to ‘text’.
```{julia}
function setlabels(df, label)
  data = select(df, :id, :data_x => :text)
  data[!, :label] .= label
  return data
end

negatives = setlabels(negatives, 0)
self_harm = setlabels(self_harm, 4)
# and so on for all of them
all_texts = vcat(negatives, self_harm, ) # etc for all the classes
```


Write out the single-classification data
Now we can export, and I do this both for CSV and parquet.
```{julia}
CSV.write(datadir("exp_pro", "all_texts.csv"), all_texts, header=true, append=false)
write_parquet(datadir("exp_pro", "all_texts.parquet"), all_texts)
```


Build the model and examine
The model (or actually a number of scikit-learn models) was built in python, for which I could use PythonCall, but let’s skip that part. This is about handling data, not building models.I could also use Scikitlearn.jl to build the models directly in Julia.
What I found is that the accuracy was very poor for self-harm, because there were far fewer instances in the dataset. I decided to remove this classification for now, and build a model without it. This is straightforward. In addition, there was a large imbalance between negatives and all the positive classifications, which means that the balanced accuracy score was significantly lower than the overall accuracy score. I decided to downsample the negatives to bring the numbers roughly in line with the others.
```{julia}
negs = negatives[sample(1:nrow(negatives), 5_700, replace=false), :]
reduced_texts = vcat(negs, eating_disorders, ) # etc
```
And write out the files once more.


Split into train/validation/test sets
This worked well for scikit-learn models. I also wanted to build a Distilbert model using hugging-face transformers. Scikit-learn has a nice feature to split test-train and then uses cross-validation, but hugging face apparently does not do cross-validation. I therefore split the training set into a train/validation set.
```{julia}
shuffled_df = Dataframe(shuffle(eachrow(reduced_texts)))
train_size = Int(round(nrow(shuffled_df) * 0.8))
mh_train = shuffled_df[1:train_size, :]
mh_test = shuffled_df[train_size + 1:end, :]

valid_size = Int(round(nrow(mh_train) * 0.85))
valid_df = mh_train[valid_size + 1:end, :]
mh_train = mh_train[1:valid_size, :]
```
These dataframes were then written out, loaded onto Databricks, and a Distilbert model built.

title: Dealing with multi-class ML data
text:
Multi-label classifier
We have data that has multiple labels associated with the same text where appropriate. There were nothing like as many as I was expecting, but worth seeing whether building a one-vs-rest model that took account of all the labels would do a good job. This is not so straightforward, however, because now we have to parse each part of the label, taking account of inconsistencies like missing quotes, periods inside the label, etc, and convert the strings to integers.
The first thing is to take account of the inconsistent names (‘weapons’ vs ‘weapon’, ‘self-harm’ vs ‘self harm’, etc). I did this by making a dictionary mapping the strings to integers, and simply added extra items for variants, mapping to the same integers.
```{julia}
policy_names = Dict(
  "negative" == 0,
  "eating disorder" == 1,
  "suicide" == 2,
  "sucide" == 2 # and so on for all the classifications and all the variants
  ) 
```
Given a string such as “[‘class1’, ‘class3’…]” We can extract each policy name, strip extra characters, look up the label numbers, and return an array of integers. Optionally exclude any policies we don’t want at this time (eg self-harm).
```{julia}
function findpolicy(str, exclusions=[])
  isdelim(char) = char == '.' || char == ','
  splits = split(str, isdelim)
  items = map(x -> strip(x, [ '[', ']', ' ', ''', '"', '.' ]), splits)
  result = map(item -> policy_names(lowercase(item)), items)
  return setdiff!(result, exclusions)
end

coded_df = @chain df begin
  @rtransform(:labels = findpolicy(:Final_Label))
  select(:id, :data_x => :text, :labels)
end
```
To load it into pandas. I converted to JSON. We can use JSONTables for this
```{julia}
jsonstring = arraytable(coded_df)
open(datadir("exp_pro", "multiclass_captures_texts.json"), "w") do f
  write(f, jsonstring)
end
```
Finally, I made a reduced version of the multiclass to exclude self-harm. One addition here is that we need to guard against cases where self-harm is the only label for a string.
```{julia}
reduced_df = @chain df begin
  @rtransform(:labels = findpolicy(:Final_Label, [4]))
  select(:id, :data_x => :text, :labels)
  @rsubset(:labels != [])
end
```
And that’s it! As always, I was impressed by the power of Julia dataframes and macros to do a great deal in very few lines, and it runs fast. In practice, I use whatever language seems to best suit the task at hand, whether that be Python, R, Julia, or SQL. My favourite is Julia, but that isn’t available on Databricks. For statistics (including Bayesian models) I generally prefer R, and I also like the geocomputing setup on R. All three are good at graphics, although some have facilities that others don’t, but most of the time I will use ggplot2 in R or Makie in Julia, but Seaborn is also fine, and I like Folium. Python still leads the pack on ML libraries, with both scikit-learn and huggingface being indispensible.
